current_episode.title: The Otago Opportunity - Episode 13 - Asset Management

guest.bio_context: Murray Pugh is the CEO of Apopo, the lead professional association for Aotearoa New Zealand's infrastructure asset management community. He leads an organisation with 1,300 members and is responsible for advancing professionalisation and accreditation in asset management across New Zealand. Under his leadership, Apopo established the Asset Management Chartered Professional designation, which has been recognised by the World Partners in Asset Management as equivalent to their global certification scheme.

context.real_quote: Unless we invest now, and maybe forego something else, then our children and our grandchildren are going to shoulder a very highly disproportional impact from failing infrastructure.
key_stats: Apopo has 1,300 members in New Zealand, of whom approximately 55% are from local government and only around 7% from central government asset owners

OECD research published in 2023: New Zealand ranked 29th out of 33 OECD countries for infrastructure governance overall, and dead last (33rd out of 33) for accountability and professionalisation in asset management
12 out of 31 central government agencies in New Zealand do not have a basic asset register, according to the National Infrastructure Plan released in 2025
Infrastructure Commission Te Wahananga: for every dollar spent on infrastructure, 60 cents must go to maintenance and renewals, leaving only 40 cents for new construction
In New Zealand's health sector, annual maintenance spending is well below 2% of asset value, compared to an international benchmark closer to 5% of asset value per year
Apopo survey of 50 senior practitioners: 70% ranked governance as the highest priority for improving asset management in New Zealand

Post-World War II infrastructure boom lasted approximately 30 years; much of New Zealand's infrastructure built in the 1950s and 1960s had a planned life cycle of around 50 years and has not been systematically replaced
context.transcript_excerpt: Coming up on the Otago Opportunity, we're talking to Murray Pugh from Apopo about the very important topic of infrastructure and asset management. This is the Otago Opportunity, a limited series look at the future of our province. I'm your host, Pauline Moore, and in this series, we're taking the policies of the Opportunity Party and moving them out of the Wellington think tank and into our own backyard here in Dunedin. Each week we'll hear from local business owners, students, and families about how a tax reset or a citizens' assembly would actually impact their daily lives. It's not about the politics, it's about the future of the place we call home. Welcome to the Otago Opportunity. Kia ora, and welcome to the Otago Opportunity. Joining me today is Dave Bainbridge-Zappa, the Opportunity candidate for Dunedin. Welcome Dave. Kia ora. And our guest, Murray Pugh, CEO for Apopo. Thank you for taking the time to come and chat with us, Murray. Hello Pauline, great to be here, David. The management of our infrastructure, so our roads, water pipes, buildings, is obviously hugely important in New Zealand, both for our economy and for our population's wellbeing, and with concerns about climate resilience and energy security really upfront in people's minds. Murray, you're the CEO for Apopo, which is the lead professional association for Aotearoa New Zealand's infrastructure asset management community. That's quite a mouthful. So your members are the people who manage these infrastructure assets. Is that right? Yes, it is. It's the really quite passionate and talented people who have that responsibility, that accountability for ensuring that our infrastructure delivers the services that our communities expect. So what I mean by that, if you think of a bridge, it connects communities. It's not just a piece of steel or concrete. It's a passageway for people and things, goods, to move between places. So communities have an expectation that bridges will perform that function. Sometimes they might like the look of it, but primarily they need that infrastructure to perform its function and deliver service. And we've certainly seen that recently when the road isn't there or the bridge isn't there. What happens to communities? Absolutely. And to things like the economy and to, as you mentioned, overall well-being. So we often think about the four well-beings of social, cultural, economic and environmental. Asset management, infrastructure asset management, is something which seeks to balance all of those well-beings for the best possible outcome and to deliver the quality of life that we all strive to have. So what's involved in that when you say asset management, what are you actually doing? It sounds like it's a huge job. It is a huge job and it's obviously really important. What was involved is thinking about what services communities need. So I'll carry on with the bridge example. So two communities on different sides of the river need to be connected to each other. And so an asset manager might try and work out, well, what's the best way of achieving that connection? What's the way that those communities can afford to have that connection? Is it a boat across the river? Is it a bridge? And then working through design and construction and bringing that asset, whether it's a boat or bridge, to fruition so that it begins its service. And then really importantly, looking after that asset over its whole planned life cycle. And for a bridge, often that's somewhere between 50 and 100 years. We've certainly got bridges well beyond that age around New Zealand. And putting in place the plans and executing on those plans, which ensure that that bridge is maintained, the asset is maintained to a level where it continues to provide the services which the communities need. So over time, the bridge gets older and it might need its deck replaced because it's too rough for modern vehicles to travel over. So that would be part of the asset management funct

pending_qa.q: What is the problem of deferred maintenance and how has it affected New Zealand's infrastructure?
pending_qa.r: Deferred maintenance refers to the repeated postponement of scheduled maintenance, often driven by short political cycles such as New Zealand's three-year election cycle, where decisions are delayed to avoid costs in the current term. Much of New Zealand's infrastructure was built during the post-World War II boom of the 1950s and 1960s, typically with a life cycle of around 50 years, and has not been adequately maintained or replaced since. The result is that New Zealand now faces a situation where ageing infrastructure is deteriorating simultaneously, leaving future generations — children and grandchildren — to bear disproportionate costs.

pending_qa.q: How does Canada serve as a model for improving infrastructure asset management capability nationally?
pending_qa.r: Canada's federal government channelled funding to improve asset management capability across the country through its provincial governments over a seven-year funding period, significantly increasing both the competence of individual practitioners and the overall number of qualified people available. This targeted investment in capability development is cited as an international example of how structured federal funding can systematically raise standards nationwide. Murray Pugh highlighted this model in contrast to New Zealand's fragmented and underfunded approach.

pending_qa.q: How do te ao Māori principles connect to internationally recognised best practice in infrastructure asset management?
pending_qa.r: Murray Pugh explained that the principles of te ao Māori align closely with globally recognised best practice in asset management, particularly around long-term thinking. Iwi and hapū are known to operate with 100-year planning horizons as a baseline, whereas local government struggles with 10- or 30-year plans and central government is only beginning to adopt such timeframes for infrastructure planning. Apopo actively incorporates te ao Māori knowledge systems into its guidance and training materials alongside ISO 55,000 international standards.

pending_qa.q: Why is governance identified as the biggest priority for improving asset management in New Zealand?
pending_qa.r: Apopo conducted a survey of 50 of its most senior practitioners in New Zealand, and 70% of them ranked governance as the highest priority for improving asset management in the country. The core issue is that decision-makers at the board and council level lack sufficient asset management competence, leading to deferred decisions, avoidance of necessary maintenance investment, and preference for visible new projects over less photogenic upkeep. Apopo's response includes developing micro-credentials and learning resources specifically targeted at elected officials and governance-level leaders.

pending_qa.q: What is the significance of the new Dunedin Hospital as an infrastructure project in New Zealand?
pending_qa.r: The new Dunedin Hospital is described as the biggest civil engineering project in New Zealand since the Clyde Dam, reflecting how little major infrastructure has been built in the country for decades. The decision to build a new hospital rather than refurbish the existing one was driven by the finding that refurbishment costs would have run into the billions, making new construction more cost-effective. However, concern was raised that cuts to the capital budget during construction will increase future maintenance costs, repeating the same pattern of under-investment.
